error_modes.label: Altitude control and level-off in the descent

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check with attention held on the navigation display, did not monitor the altimeter through the descent and did not anticipate the level-off. SP passed the cleared altitude by more than 300 feet and continued descending until IP intervened with control inputs to arrest the descent. SP did not initiate any recovery on his/her own and the aircraft state was not restored without assistance.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check that left the altimeter outside the scan for long intervals, did not lead the level-off with a timely power reduction and pitch change. Deviation from the cleared altitude reached the 300 feet limit and SP corrected only after repeated verbal prompting by IP. The recovery was late and the altitude was regained slowly.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that dwelled on the navigation instruments at the expense of the altimeter, allowed the vertical profile to run ahead of the intended one. Altitude deviation grew past 150 feet and reached approximately 200 to 250 feet before SP detected it. SP corrected in good time and returned to the cleared altitude without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained an active instrument cross-check that kept the altimeter in the scan throughout the descent. Altitude was held within 150 feet of the cleared and intermediate altitudes, and the level-off was led with a timely power and pitch change. Corrections were prompt and precise.
texts.4: SP flew the en-route descent with a continuous and evenly distributed cross-check, holding altitude essentially on the cleared values with negligible excursions. The level-off was anticipated and executed with no perceptible overshoot. Vertical profile control was of a standard well above the level expected at this stage.
texts.marginal: SP kept altitude within tolerance during the en-route descent, but the deviations clustered toward the outer part of the acceptable band and were consistently on the low side approaching level-off. SP corrected each time before any prompting, yet the cross-check returned to the altimeter later than desirable. SP is expected to tighten the vertical scan and lead the level-off earlier so that altitude control is centered rather than marginal.

texts.0: SP, due to setting descent power without reference to the pitch attitude required for the target airspeed, allowed the airspeed to diverge and did not arrest the trend. Airspeed departed the briefed value by more than 20 KIAS and continued to increase, so IP intervened on the power lever to recover the parameter. SP did not recognize the divergence from the airspeed indicator in time.
texts.1: SP, due to a power setting that did not match the selected descent attitude, did not stabilize the airspeed at the briefed value. Airspeed deviation reached the 20 KIAS limit and was corrected only after IP called it verbally. The subsequent correction was coarse and the airspeed settled slowly.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power adjustment after establishing the descent attitude, permitted the airspeed to drift from the briefed value. The deviation exceeded 10 KIAS and reached approximately 15 KIAS before SP recognized it. SP restored the airspeed in good time with a smooth power change and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP established the descent with a power setting and attitude matched to the briefed airspeed and held the parameter within 10 KIAS throughout. Small deviations were detected early and corrected with smooth, measured power changes. Airspeed control remained stable through the level-off.
texts.4: SP controlled airspeed with negligible deviation from the briefed descent value from entry to level-off. Power and attitude were coordinated so precisely that no corrective input larger than a small power adjustment was required. Airspeed control was of a very high standard.
texts.marginal: SP held airspeed within tolerance, but the values sat persistently toward the fast side of the acceptable band and the trend was not fully arrested until late in the descent. SP recognized and corrected without assistance on each occasion. SP is expected to set descent power more decisively at entry so that airspeed remains centered on the briefed value rather than close to the outer limit.

error_modes.label: Heading and course keeping during the descent

texts.0: SP, due to uncorrected trim and inattention to the heading indicator while managing the descent, allowed a continuous drift off the assigned heading. The deviation exceeded 10 degrees and continued to grow away from the cleared track, so IP intervened to return the aircraft to heading. SP did not detect the divergence unaided.
texts.1: SP, due to bank inputs that were not held steady while the power was being adjusted, did not maintain the assigned heading during the descent. Heading deviation reached the 10 degree limit and was corrected only after IP pointed it out. The correction was overcontrolled and required a second adjustment to settle.
texts.2: SP, due to an out-of-trim condition following the power reduction, allowed the aircraft to drift off the assigned heading. The deviation passed 5 degrees and reached approximately 7 to 8 degrees before SP noticed it. SP corrected promptly with a shallow, coordinated turn and regained the assigned heading without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned heading within 5 degrees throughout the en-route descent, including during power and configuration changes. Corrections were small, coordinated and applied as soon as a trend appeared. Directional control remained steady through the level-off.
texts.4: SP held the assigned heading essentially on value for the whole descent, with excursions that were barely perceptible on the instrument. Turns to new headings were rolled out on target without oscillation. Directional control was consistently precise.
texts.marginal: SP kept heading within tolerance, but the aircraft was allowed to wander repeatedly to one side of the assigned value before each correction. SP detected and fixed the drift without prompting, although the corrections were reactive rather than anticipatory. SP is expected to keep the aircraft trimmed after each power change so that heading is held rather than repeatedly recaptured.

error_modes.label: ATC clearance compliance and readback for the descent

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete readback that left the assigned descent altitude unconfirmed, began the en-route descent to an altitude that was not the one cleared by ATC. SP did not comply with the ATC instruction and did not query the controller when the instruction was unclear. IP intervened, took the radios and stopped the descent before the aircraft continued below the cleared level.
texts.1: SP, due to a readback that omitted the altitude restriction issued with the clearance, did not comply fully with the ATC descent instruction. SP began the descent late and to the wrong intermediate level, and complied only after IP restated the clearance verbally. The resulting altitude deviation reached the 300 feet limit before the correct profile was resumed.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried readback made while still adjusting the descent power, misheard part of the ATC instruction. SP started the descent with the wrong initial rate but recognized the discrepancy, requested confirmation from the controller on his/her own initiative and complied correctly. The resulting altitude deviation stayed between 150 and 300 feet and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP read back the descent clearance completely and accurately, including the assigned altitude and any restriction, and complied with the ATC instruction without delay. Radio work did not interfere with aircraft control and all parameters remained within tolerance during the exchange. Coordination with the controller was clear and standard.
texts.4: SP handled the ATC descent clearance with a concise, complete readback and immediate, exact compliance, while flight parameters remained essentially unaffected. SP anticipated the clearance and was prepared for the descent before it was issued. Radio discipline and compliance were of a very high standard.
texts.marginal: SP complied with the ATC descent clearance and the readback contained all mandatory elements, but the phraseology was hesitant and the compliance action followed the instruction later than expected. Parameters stayed within tolerance during the radio work. SP is expected to consolidate standard phraseology so that clearances are read back and acted upon without hesitation.

error_modes.label: Routing and altitude restrictions from MAIP and approach manuals

texts.0: SP, due to not having reviewed the published route and altitude restrictions for the arrival before commencing the descent, violated a published minimum altitude segment. SP descended below the published level by more than 300 feet and showed no awareness of the restriction. IP intervened to level the aircraft and to restore the published profile.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete review of the MAIP and approach manual data, did not respect a published altitude restriction on the arrival. SP arrived at the restriction point at the 300 feet limit off the published altitude and corrected only after IP identified the restriction verbally. The published routing was regained late.
texts.2: SP, due to referring to the published restrictions only after the descent had begun, planned the descent rate against the wrong crossing point. Altitude at the restriction point was between 150 and 300 feet off the published value, but SP identified the error, adjusted the descent rate and complied at the following segment without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP flew the en-route descent within the routing and altitude restrictions published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals. Crossing altitudes were planned before commencing the descent and met within 150 feet. No restriction was violated at any point.
texts.4: SP applied the published routing and altitude restrictions with full accuracy, crossing every constraint point essentially on the published value. The descent rate was planned in advance so that no late adjustment was needed. Knowledge and application of the published data were of an exemplary standard.
texts.marginal: SP respected all published routing and altitude restrictions, but crossing altitudes were met with little margin and the descent rate was adjusted late at more than one segment. No restriction was violated and no assistance was needed. SP is expected to plan the descent profile earlier so that published constraints are met with a comfortable margin rather than marginally.

error_modes.label: Standardized descent procedure and sequence without IP intervention

texts.0: SP, due to not applying the descent sequence described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3, omitted the descent checks and configured the aircraft out of order. The omissions accumulated and the aircraft was left in a state that required IP to take control and re-establish the correct procedure. SP did not execute the descent without mistakes or without IP intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to an unrehearsed descent flow, performed the required actions out of the standardized sequence and omitted one item until reminded. SP completed the procedure only after IP prompted each remaining step verbally. Flight parameters reached the outer limits, with altitude at 300 feet off the assigned value, while SP was catching up with the sequence.
texts.2: SP, due to starting the descent checks after rather than before initiating the descent, executed part of the sequence out of order. SP recognized the omission unaided, went back and completed the missing items correctly. Parameters remained between the code 3 and code 1 bands, with altitude no worse than 250 feet off, and IP did not intervene.
texts.3: SP executed the en-route descent according to the standardized procedures of the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3, in the correct sequence and without mistakes. Descent checks were completed before entering the descent and no item was omitted. No IP intervention was required at any stage.
texts.4: SP flew the en-route descent to a standardized flow that was complete, correctly ordered and unhurried, with every check accomplished ahead of the point where it was needed. The procedure was executed flawlessly and left ample capacity for aircraft control and navigation. Procedural execution was of an exemplary standard.
texts.marginal: SP executed the descent procedure correctly and in sequence, but the flow was slow and each step was completed close to the point at which it was needed. No item was omitted and no prompting was required. SP is expected to rehearse the descent flow so that the procedure is completed with margin rather than at the last available moment.

error_modes.label: Radio navigation aid use and orientation during the descent

texts.0: SP, due to a loss of awareness of the aircraft position relative to the navigation facility, did not tune, identify or correctly interpret the radio aid used for the en-route descent. SP became disoriented as to position along the route and continued the descent on an incorrect track. IP intervened to re-establish orientation and to return the aircraft to the cleared routing.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete picture of the aircraft position relative to the facility, did not use the radio aid to maintain orientation during the descent. SP required IP to state the position and the required track before continuing. The resulting heading deviation reached the 10 degree limit and the track was regained only after the verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed update of the navigation picture after the descent was commenced, misread the position relative to the facility. SP identified the error from the raw data unaided, re-established orientation and returned to the correct track. Heading deviation stayed between 5 and 10 degrees and no IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP tuned and identified the radio aids correctly and used them to maintain accurate orientation throughout the en-route descent. Position relative to the facility was known at all times and the aircraft was flown on the cleared track within 5 degrees. SP demonstrated a clear navigation picture without assistance.
texts.4: SP used the radio navigation aids with full accuracy, maintaining an unbroken awareness of position along the route and of the distance and altitude required at each point. Orientation was never in doubt and SP could state the required action to reach the destination or the alternate at any moment. Navigation awareness was of a very high standard.
texts.marginal: SP maintained orientation with the radio aids and flew the cleared track within tolerance, but the navigation picture was rebuilt by repeated checks rather than held continuously. SP answered position questions correctly, though after a noticeable delay. SP is expected to keep the navigation picture updated throughout the descent so that orientation is immediate rather than reconstructed.

error_modes.label: Power management and rate of descent

texts.0: SP, due to not controlling engine power in accordance with the phase of flight as required by the Flight Manual, set a descent power that produced a rate of descent unsuited to the clearance. SP made no adjustment as the profile diverged and the aircraft arrived at the level-off far outside the required altitude, more than 300 feet off. IP intervened on the power lever to control the descent rate.
texts.1: SP, due to a descent power setting selected without reference to the distance and altitude to be lost, flew a rate of descent that did not match the required profile. SP adjusted the power only after IP called the discrepancy, and the resulting altitude error reached the 300 feet limit at the level-off point. The correction was late and coarse.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction that was smaller than required at descent entry, established a rate of descent below the one needed for the profile. SP detected the shortfall on the vertical picture, increased the rate in good time and met the level-off with an error between 150 and 300 feet. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP controlled engine power appropriately for the descent phase, producing a rate of descent matched to the distance and altitude to be lost. Power changes were smooth and within the Flight Manual limits, and the level-off was met with altitude within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 KIAS. The profile required no significant correction.
texts.4: SP managed engine power throughout the en-route descent with precision, selecting a rate of descent that met the profile exactly and required only minimal refinement. Power changes were smooth, anticipatory and always within limits. Energy management during the descent was of an exemplary standard.
texts.marginal: SP managed power adequately and kept the descent within the required profile, but the rate of descent needed several corrections and the power changes were larger than necessary. All parameters remained within tolerance without assistance. SP is expected to select the correct descent power at entry so that the rate is set once rather than repeatedly adjusted.

error_modes.label: Trim handling through the descent and level-off

texts.0: SP, due to leaving the aircraft out of trim after the power reduction and the airspeed change, flew the descent against sustained control forces. The out-of-trim condition led to continuous divergence in pitch and heading beyond 300 feet and 10 degrees, and SP was unable to hold the parameters. IP intervened to trim the aircraft and to restore controlled flight.
texts.1: SP, due to not retrimming elevator and rudder as the airspeed changed in the descent, held the aircraft with constant control pressure and was unable to fly it with comfort and ease. Deviations reached the 300 feet and 10 degree limits and were corrected only after IP prompted SP to trim. The aircraft was stabilized late.
texts.2: SP, due to trimming only in pitch and neglecting rudder trim after the power change, allowed the aircraft to fly slightly out of balance in the descent. Heading drift passed 5 degrees and altitude control became irregular within the 150 to 300 feet band. SP recognized the condition, completed the trimming correctly and restored stable flight without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP trimmed the aircraft correctly in pitch, roll and yaw as power and airspeed changed during the descent and at the level-off. The aircraft was flown with comfort and ease and remained essentially hands-off between corrections. Parameters were held within 150 feet and 5 degrees throughout.
texts.4: SP kept the aircraft accurately trimmed across the full airspeed range of the descent, retrimming immediately after each power or attitude change. The aircraft was flown almost entirely on trim with negligible control pressures and negligible parameter excursions. Trim handling was of a very high standard.
texts.marginal: SP trimmed the aircraft and kept all parameters within tolerance, but the retrimming followed each power change later than it should and residual control pressures were evident during the level-off. SP required no prompting and corrected the condition unaided. SP is expected to retrim promptly with every power and airspeed change so that the aircraft is flown on trim rather than held on the controls.

error_modes.label: Start-down point computation for the en-route descent

texts.0: SP, due to not applying the 2:1 descent planning ratio with the extra 10 miles added for the instrument approach, did not determine a start-down point and requested the descent well inside the distance required. The descent that followed was steep and compressed, and at the point the aircraft was required to be level it was more than 300 feet from the cleared altitude with airspeed more than 20 KIAS from the planned figure. IP took control of pitch and power to salvage the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to a start-down point estimated without the technique of twice the altitude to lose in thousands of feet plus 10 miles, began the descent later than the profile allowed. The gradient had to be steepened, and at the level-off the altitude error reached the 300 feet limit while airspeed sat at the 20 KIAS limit. SP re-planned the descent only after repeated verbal prompting by IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a start-down point judged by feel rather than by the 2:1 ratio with 10 miles added, entered the descent slightly late. SP recognized the compression early, increased the gradient in good time and held the altitude error between 150 and 300 feet with airspeed between 10 and 20 KIAS of the planned value. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP computed the start-down point with the 2:1 ratio plus the 10 miles allowed for the approach and requested the descent at the appropriate distance. The profile ran without compression, altitude was held within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 KIAS at every check point. The few adjustments required were smooth and timely.
texts.4: SP determined the start-down point precisely with the 2:1 planning ratio and the additional 10 miles, and obtained a clearance that matched the desired descent profile. The descent was flown without a single significant correction, with altitude and airspeed essentially on the planned values throughout. Descent planning was of an exemplary standard.
texts.marginal: SP applied the 2:1 planning ratio but did so late, so the descent was started close to the last usable point and the gradient had to be flown at the steep end. All deviations remained inside tolerance, with altitude running consistently on the high side in the first part of the descent. SP is expected to compute the start-down point earlier and request the descent so that the profile is flown at a comfortable gradient.

error_modes.label: Pitch selection by the 60-to-1 rule for the required descent gradient

texts.0: SP, due to selecting a nose-low attitude without computing the pitch change from altitude to lose in hundreds of feet divided by the miles available, set a gradient unrelated to the one required. The vertical profile diverged progressively and altitude was more than 300 feet from the required value at the restriction, with airspeed more than 20 KIAS from the planned figure. IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to a descent attitude chosen without the 60-to-1 computation, flew a gradient that did not match the distance remaining. IP called the divergence twice before SP adjusted pitch, and altitude at the check point reached the 300 feet limit. The correction was coarse and airspeed drifted to the 20 KIAS limit while it was made.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial pitch set one to two degrees away from the value given by the 60-to-1 rule, flew a shallow gradient in the first part of the descent. SP compared the profile with the requirement, corrected pitch in good time and kept the altitude error between 150 and 300 feet. Airspeed stayed between 10 and 20 KIAS of the planned value and no IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP computed the pitch change from altitude to lose in hundreds of feet divided by the miles to go and set that attitude at descent entry. The gradient matched the requirement, altitude was held within 150 feet of the profile and airspeed within 10 KIAS. Pitch refinements were small and made before any divergence developed.
texts.4: SP applied the 60-to-1 relationship accurately, working from the fact that every degree of pitch gives 100 feet per nautical mile, and flew the computed attitude with negligible error. Altitude tracked the intended profile essentially exactly and airspeed remained on the planned value. Vertical navigation was well above the standard expected at this stage.
texts.marginal: SP used the 60-to-1 rule but rounded the computation coarsely, so the initial attitude needed two further adjustments before the required gradient was held. Altitude and airspeed remained within tolerance, with the errors sitting toward the outer part of the acceptable band. SP is expected to compute the pitch change accurately at descent entry so the attitude is set once and thereafter only refined.

error_modes.label: Verification of the descent gradient by VSI cross-check

texts.0: SP, due to not verifying the descent gradient by cross-checking the VSI against groundspeed in miles per minute and the selected gradient, flew a rate of descent that did not correspond to the profile believed to be set. The error went undetected for the whole descent and the aircraft reached the level-off more than 300 feet from the cleared altitude. IP intervened with pitch and power inputs to arrest the descent.
texts.1: SP, due to omitting the VSI cross-check that converts groundspeed and descent gradient into an expected rate, did not confirm the profile at any point of the descent. The discrepancy grew until altitude reached the 300 feet limit, and SP corrected only after IP called for a rate check. The return to the profile was slow and required a marked pitch change.
texts.2: SP, due to a VSI cross-check made well after descent entry rather than at it, flew several thousand feet before confirming that the rate matched the computed figure. By then the altitude error had grown to between 150 and 300 feet, after which SP corrected in good time and unassisted. The remainder of the descent tracked the profile.
texts.3: SP verified the descent gradient by cross-checking the VSI against groundspeed and the selected gradient shortly after descent entry. The profile was held with altitude within 150 feet at every check point and airspeed within 10 KIAS. Corrections were small and made before any divergence could develop.
texts.4: SP computed the expected rate of descent from groundspeed and gradient and verified it on the VSI without prompting, repeating the check as the descent progressed. The aircraft tracked the intended profile with negligible error and required no significant correction. Cross-check of the vertical profile was of an exemplary standard.
texts.marginal: SP did cross-check the VSI against the computed rate, but only some way into the descent, so the first part of the profile was flown unverified. Deviations stayed within tolerance while sitting toward the outer part of the band. SP is expected to confirm the rate of descent against groundspeed and gradient immediately after descent entry.

error_modes.label: Updating the descent profile for the effect of wind on rate of descent

texts.0: SP, due to computing the required rate of descent from planned airspeed without allowing for the wind, held a rate suited to no-wind conditions while a substantial tailwind raised the groundspeed. The gradient flattened, the descent fell behind the profile and the aircraft was more than 300 feet high at the point the restriction applied, with airspeed more than 20 KIAS from the planned figure during the hurried deceleration. IP intervened to correct the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to not updating the descent profile for the reported wind, did not adjust the target rate when the headwind reduced groundspeed. The descent ran ahead of the intended profile, altitude deviation reached the 300 feet limit and SP corrected only after repeated IP prompting. The deceleration and configuration that followed were rushed.
texts.2: SP, due to a rate of descent computed from the planned groundspeed rather than the actual one, allowed a wind-induced error to build in the vertical profile. SP noticed the drift when comparing distance against altitude to lose, adjusted the rate in good time and kept the altitude error between 150 and 300 feet. Airspeed stayed between 10 and 20 KIAS of the planned value throughout.
texts.3: SP accounted for the effect of the wind on groundspeed and adjusted the target rate of descent accordingly, holding the selected gradient. Altitude was kept within 150 feet of the profile and airspeed within 10 KIAS, and the deceleration was unhurried. Updates to the rate were smooth and timely.
texts.4: SP anticipated the wind effect on groundspeed, adjusted the target rate of descent before any divergence appeared and held the planned gradient exactly. Altitude and airspeed tracked the profile with negligible error and the deceleration was entirely unhurried. Allowance for wind in the descent was of a standard well above that expected at this stage.
texts.marginal: SP allowed for the wind but used a groundspeed figure that was not refreshed during the descent, so the rate had to be corrected twice as the profile progressed. All deviations remained within tolerance, consistently on the high side of the intended altitudes. SP is expected to update groundspeed during the descent and adjust the rate accordingly rather than correcting after the error has appeared.

error_modes.label: Use of the known pitch and power settings for the 200 KIAS descent

texts.0: SP, due to not using the known descent settings that pair degrees nose-low with torque to hold 200 KIAS, set an arbitrary attitude and power combination at descent entry. Airspeed diverged and settled more than 20 KIAS from the descent speed while altitude ran more than 300 feet from the intended profile. IP intervened on the power lever and stick to restore the descent.
texts.1: SP, due to a pitch and power combination not taken from the known descent settings, chased airspeed with repeated power changes through the descent. Airspeed deviation reached the 20 KIAS limit and altitude reached the 300 feet limit before SP acted on IP prompting. The whole descent was flown with coarse and continuous corrections.
texts.2: SP, due to a torque setting that did not match the nose-low attitude selected for the descent, allowed airspeed to move away from 200 KIAS. SP recalled the correct pitch and power pairing, reset it in good time and held the airspeed error between 10 and 20 KIAS with altitude between 150 and 300 feet of the profile. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP set the known combination of nose-low attitude and torque for a 200 KIAS descent at entry and held it through the descent. Airspeed remained within 10 KIAS and altitude within 150 feet of the profile, with only minor refinements to power. The descent was smooth and efficient.
texts.4: SP applied the known pitch and power settings for the descent immediately and accurately, so that 200 KIAS was established without any chasing of the airspeed indicator. Airspeed and altitude tracked the profile with negligible deviation for the whole descent. Use of the standard settings was of an exemplary standard.
texts.marginal: SP used the known pitch and power pairing but set the torque only approximately, so airspeed needed three separate power adjustments before it settled at the descent speed. Deviations remained within tolerance while sitting toward the outer part of the band. SP is expected to set the exact torque for the nose-low attitude chosen so that airspeed stabilizes at the first attempt.

error_modes.label: Airspeed restriction below 10,000 feet MSL during the descent

texts.0: SP, due to steepening the gradient to make a published altitude restriction without adjusting airspeed for it, exceeded 250 KIAS below 10,000 feet MSL and made no power reduction to recover the limit. The excursion continued and airspeed reached more than 20 KIAS above the descent speed while the profile was flown steeply. IP intervened on the power lever and speed brake to bring the aircraft back within limits.
texts.1: SP, due to a steepened descent gradient flown without a matching power reduction, accelerated toward 250 KIAS below 10,000 feet MSL. SP retarded the power only after IP called the speed, and the airspeed excursion reached the 20 KIAS limit from the descent speed. The recovery required speed brake and a marked pitch change.
texts.2: SP, due to increasing the descent gradient without anticipating the acceleration that follows, allowed airspeed to rise as the aircraft approached 10,000 feet MSL. SP detected the trend before the restriction applied, used power and speed brake in good time and kept the airspeed error between 10 and 20 KIAS. The 250 KIAS limit was not exceeded and no IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP managed airspeed against the 250 KIAS restriction below 10,000 feet MSL, adjusting power and speed brake as the gradient was changed to meet the published restrictions. Airspeed stayed within 10 KIAS of the descent speed and the limit was respected with margin. Adjustments were smooth and anticipatory.
texts.4: SP anticipated the acceleration associated with each gradient change and kept airspeed comfortably clear of the 250 KIAS restriction below 10,000 feet MSL. Airspeed held essentially on the descent value with negligible variation and speed brake was used sparingly and precisely. Speed control against the published restriction was well above the standard expected.
texts.marginal: SP remained below 250 KIAS through the lower part of the descent, but airspeed was allowed to sit close to the restriction and speed brake had to be held to contain it. All values remained within tolerance with a clear tendency toward the fast side. SP is expected to set the gradient and power so that the margin below the restriction is kept without continuous speed brake use.

error_modes.label: Planning the descent to allow unhurried deceleration and configuration before the FAF

texts.0: SP, due to not planning the descent so the aircraft could be configured before the FAF, arrived at the approach segment high and fast with the whole deceleration still to be made. The attempt to lose altitude and speed together left the aircraft more than 300 feet from the required altitude and more than 20 KIAS from the required speed. IP intervened to configure the aircraft and stabilize the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to a descent profile that left no allowance for deceleration before the FAF, delayed the speed reduction until the final part of the descent. The deceleration was hurried, altitude deviation reached the 300 feet limit and airspeed reached the 20 KIAS limit before SP acted on IP prompting. Configuration was completed late.
texts.2: SP, due to starting the deceleration later than the planned profile allowed, compressed the transition from descent speed to approach speed. SP recognized the compression, reduced power in good time and completed the configuration with altitude between 150 and 300 feet and airspeed between 10 and 20 KIAS of the required values. The approach was flown without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP planned the descent so that deceleration and configuration were completed before the FAF without haste. Altitude was within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 KIAS at the point of configuration, and the power reduction was smooth. The transition into the approach was orderly.
texts.4: SP planned the descent so that the aircraft was decelerated and configured well before the FAF with no compression at any stage. Altitude and airspeed at configuration were essentially on the required values and the transition into the approach was seamless. Descent planning for the approach was of an exemplary standard.
texts.marginal: SP was configured before the FAF, but the deceleration was begun late and had to be completed with a rapid power reduction. All parameters stayed within tolerance, with airspeed on the fast side until shortly before configuration. SP is expected to plan the descent so that the speed reduction begins early enough for an unhurried configuration.
